core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: The empirical effect is among the most reproducible in memory research: pictures of concrete items are recognised and recalled better than their names, across decades of experiments and standard textbook treatment. Paivio's Mental Representations (1986) and Clark & Paivio's educational synthesis (1991) are both in the corpus and both pins resolved. Scored 3 for the effect; the theoretical explanation is a separate matter treated in dissent, and grade A- rather than A reflects that the mechanism's *why* is contested even where its *what* is not.

product_applicability.rationale: Directly implementable where the product has visible output: show the actual result rather than describing it; encode recurring concrete states visually. Highly relevant to Ventora's own output products, many of which produce visual artefacts. Reference: generated-output galleries, real user artefacts as explanation, status iconography.

measurability.rationale: Reachable proxies exist (conversion, engagement, recognition-driven task time), but the effect measured in the literature is *memory*, which our telemetry does not observe directly. We would be inferring from downstream behaviour, and — as with PF-16 — the same design change also alters load and comprehension, making attribution to picture superiority specifically difficult. Scored 2 honestly.

orthogonality.rationale: Frequently conflated with MM-15 in practitioner writing into a general 'visuals beat text' claim. Kept separate deliberately: PS-13 is a memory advantage for concrete depictable items; MM-15 is a set of combination rules for explanatory content. Different evidence, boundaries and failure modes — but real adjacency, hence 2.

safety.rationale: Low intrinsic hazard: showing the real thing is user-serving and typically more honest than describing it. The misuse vectors are substitution (replacing prices, terms and conditional information with imagery that cannot represent them), idealised depiction (showing outputs the product does not typically produce — straightforward deceptive advertising), and accessibility loss where image becomes the sole carrier of meaning. All three are hard rules with clear boundaries.

dissent: The effect is solid; its standard explanation is not, and the popular reading of it is wrong in a way that matters for us. (1) Theoretical contest: dual coding — separate verbal and imaginal codes giving pictures two retrieval routes — is the classic account, but it has been challenged since the imagery debates by single-system propositional accounts, and contemporary explanations often favour distinctiveness and sensory-semantic richness over the specific dual-code architecture. We therefore claim the empirical regularity and treat 'dual coding' as convenient framing rather than settled mechanism. (2) Boundary, and the one that constrains us most: the advantage is established for concrete, nameable items. Abstract concepts, conditional statements, precise quantities and sequential procedures gain nothing and lose fidelity when depicted — text is superior for exactly the content types where errors are most costly (price, terms, instructions). (3) Domain: the evidence measures recognition and recall in laboratory memory tasks, not comprehension of a commercial proposition or subsequent action. A memory advantage is not automatically a comprehension advantage and certainly not automatically a conversion advantage. (4) Corpus quality caveat, ours: the harvest for this mechanism was substantially polluted by terminological collision — 'visual processing advantage' and 'dual coding' pulled in computer-vision and coding-theory literature — so the canon here rests on the resolved pins and a minority of on-topic records rather than on a broad clean corpus. That is a reason for the incubating status and for a re-harvest with tightened terms before promotion. Taken together: this mechanism supports 'show the concrete result instead of describing it'; it does not support 'replace text with pictures', which is the reading it usually receives.

evidence_sources.ref: Paivio (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.
Clark & Paivio (1991). Dual coding theory and education. Educational Psychology Review 3(3).
